text: Every twenty-seven minutes, someone in Goa is bitten by a dog.
In 2025 alone, that was nineteen thousand, three hundred and sixty-eight bite cases.
And when you find an injured animal on the road, who do you even call?
Every municipality runs its own helpline. Some close at eight in the evening.
And last year, Canacona, Sankhalim, Valpoi and Mapusa held no sterilisation camps at all.
Meet Paw S.O.S. Goa: one WhatsApp number for every animal emergency in the state. No app to install.
Here it is, working. You send a photo of the animal, and your location.
Within seconds, Claude looks at the photo and replies: how urgent it seems, and two or three safe things to do while you wait. It is guidance, never a diagnosis.
If someone else reports the same animal nearby, Paw S.O.S. merges it into the same case. The team gets one alert, not two.
The nearest partner team gets the photo, a map link, and two buttons: accept, or decline.
If nobody answers in time, the case moves on to the next team, and then to the taluka officer. Nothing waits forever.
Accepted. On site. Resolved. And the person who reported it hears every single step.
For officials, every case sits on one map, with a full audit trail, and a suggestion for where the next sterilisation camp is needed.
Under the hood, it is one Python service and one PostGIS database.
WhatsApp, Telegram and this web demo all arrive as the same message, so they run the same logic.
One state machine owns every case and records every change. If the AI is slow, the case is routed anyway. If a message fails to send, the case is never lost.
The teams in this demo are placeholders, and the WhatsApp line is waiting on Meta's business verification. But the whole loop works today.
This is Paw S.O.S. Goa. One number. Every report heard.
